newsitem.title: CHILE: Top Chilean court rebuffs military on amnesties.
newsitem.headline: Top Chilean court rebuffs military on amnesties.

text.p: Chile's Supreme Court rejected on Thursday a demand by the armed forces that it issue guidelines on applying an amnesty law to human rights cases.
Rights activists had feared the armed forces' move was designed to speed up the application of amnesties to hundreds of cases still being dealt with by the judicial system.
The top court ruled 15-1 that individual judges must be free to decide whether to apply the military-dictated 1978 amnesty law in cases where human rights had been violated.
"Judges have the independence to make their own decisions about what rules to apply to the cases for their resolution, without outside interference," it said.

Sola Sierra, president of an association of relatives of people who were detained or who disappeared under the former military government, said, "This was the most serious situation we have faced in the last 23 years ... in which (the armed forces) have tried to close this issue without investigation."
The ruling was welcomed by lawyers, who said it underlined the court's independence and ability to resist pressure from the military, which still holds considerable power in Chile.

"The court has made an important step in confirming its credibility and its own respectability in the sense of not accepting that other powers can influence its role in fixing criteria for administering justice," human rights lawyer Nelson Caucoto said.

The amnesty law, written by Gen. Augusto Pinochet's government, covers rights violations between 1973 and 1978, a time when political violence against left-wing opponents of the government was at its height.
A government board has found that nearly 3,200 people died or disappeared without a trace during the military government's iron rule of Chile from 1973 to 1990.
